title: Microprofiling: kernel hop analysis and memory-coherence impacts on quantized inference
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

This is an investigative log capturing microprofiling experiments we ran to validate a hypothesis: quantized model inference (INT8 / FP8 / AWQ variants) amplifies kernel hop and memory-coherence effects, which in turn creates non-obvious throughput regressions and latency tail spikes even when per-kernel throughput looks fine in isolation.

High-level findings (TL;DR):
- Kernel-hopping (frequent switches between small, specialized kernels) is a dominant source of tail latency for short-context interactive workloads on quantized runtimes.
- INT8-GPTQ variants reduce computation but increase memory access intensity in hidden states (KV cache and activation staging), leading to worse L2/L3 cache eviction patterns on H100 when naive packing is used.
- AWQ-4-bit approaches show lower aggregate memory pressure but trigger more frequent code-path switches (vector-lane vs scalar fallback) in our kernel dispatcher, producing jitter in 95/99th-percentile latency.
- FP8 (e4m3) maintains better numerical locality but larger kernel sizes increase single-kernel latency; with good batching this is a win, but with tiny batch sizes this becomes worse than carefully tuned INT8.

Experiment environment and reproducibility notes:
- Hardware: H100 SXM, 80GB; A100 PCIe, 40GB for cross-checks.
- Runtime: redwood-runtime v2.7.1 (kernel-dispatcher-instrumentation branch).
- Models: Llama2-13B (hf: llm/llama2-13b), Mistral-7B (hf: llm/mistral-7b) compiled into our optimized kernels.
- Quant setups:
  * GPTQ-INT8 (per-channel weight quantization, 8-bit activations), typical autotune packing.
  * AWQ-4bit (group-wise scale + 4-bit integer), AWQ packing mode B (packed lanes).
  * FP8-e4m3 (weights cast to e4m3, fused-matmul kernels).
- Client load: synthetic interactive QPS driver (100–500 QPS), prompt lengths 8–64 tokens (most at 16 tokens), parallel clients 32.
- Measurement: integrated perf counters (SM throughput, DRAM bandwidth), NVPROF-style kernel timelines, and lightweight tracer producing per-request kernel hop sequences and timestamps.

Detailed observations:
1) Kernel hop taxonomy
- Hop type A: attention matmul small-block kernels (fast, vectorized)
- Hop type B: fused attention softmax + causal masking (memory-heavy, uses shared scratch buffers)
- Hop type C: KV cache read/write (scatter/gather like), very latency sensitive to L2 cache locality
- Hop type D: fallback scalar kernels (for odd dimension tails) — extremely slow relative to A/B

Under GPTQ-INT8 we saw an increased fraction of hops that include type C (KV scatter/gather) and D (fallback), compared to full FP32 or FP8. Why: packing for INT8 introduces uneven lane fill on smaller layers which triggers tail-handling code paths.

2) Memory-coherence patterns
- On H100 we observed frequent L2 evictions when serving many short-context requests concurrently. The INT8 case had slightly higher per-token DRAM reads (measured +9% over FP8) due to reduced compute that exposes memory latency.
- AWQ beating FP8 on aggregate bandwidth but producing more jitter in latency — hypothesis is AWQ's packed layout improves steady throughput but increases contention on shared scratch memory regions across warps.

3) Tail-latency effect amplification for small batches
- With batch size=1–2, AWQ and GPTQ show 1.6x–2.3x higher 95th latency vs FP8 on the same model. Median latency is better, but tails worsen.
- When switching to batch size=8, FP8 median degrades (larger kernels) but tails tighten and overall tokens/sec improves; the cross-over point depends on sequence length distribution.

Representative numbers (Llama2-13B, H100):
- GPTQ-INT8, bs=1, median per-token latency: 35ms, p95: 110ms, throughput (@32 parallel clients): 420 tokens/sec
- AWQ-4bit, bs=1, median: 29ms, p95: 140ms, throughput: 460 tokens/sec
- FP8-e4m3, bs=1, median: 42ms, p95: 95ms, throughput: 390 tokens/sec
- FP8-e4m3, bs=8, median: 65ms, p95: 120ms, throughput: 1100 tokens/sec
(note: these are single-run snapshots; variance across runs +/-5–12% depending on background noise)

Hypotheses for root causes:
- Dispatcher churn: frequent kernel switches (hop sequences >6 distinct kernels) incur dispatch overhead and deeper pipeline stalls in the runtime thread pool.
- Cache aliasing: packed quant layouts cause unaligned loads into scratch buffers; combined with our lane scheduling this generates inter-warp coherence churn.
- Small-layer fragmentation: quantized kernels often break larger matmuls into many smaller micro-kernels (to exploit int8 lanes) increasing kernel invocation rate.

Actionable mitigations and experiments to prioritize:
1) Aggressive hop coalescing: fuse consecutive micro-kernels in the host scheduler when they share input/output buffers. Quick prototype reduced kernel invocations by ~28% in a synthetic trace and cut p95 by ~18% in a smoke run.
2) KV cache prefetching: introduce prefetch hints and a pinned staging buffer per SM to reduce L2 churn from random access patterns. Tradeoff: increased peak DRAM allocation.
3) Lane-aware packing policy: change AWQ packing to avoid pathological alignments that hit fallback scalar kernels; this requires a packing-time pass to insert padding for small-dim layers.
4) Auto-batch hints: for interactive routes we should dynamically increase batch windows for FP8 candidates and prefer INT8/AWQ for steady high-QPS endpoints.

Notes-to-self / open questions:
- Need a longer A/B run (48h) to quantify noisy variance under cluster-level noisy neighbors.
- Confirm whether observed L2 eviction patterns persist on newer H100 firmware/driver (we tested driver v530).
- Can the jitter in AWQ be reduced by changing warp scheduling knobs in our kernel launcher (experiment id: rtm-khop-07)?
- Are there model-architectural signals (head dims, MLP split sizes) that predict which quant strategy will exacerbate hop counts? Build a small classifier.

Immediate next steps (owners and timing):
- Priya: iterate hop coalescing prototype and run full Llama2-13B/ Mistral-7B sweep (by 2028-03-22).
- Ethan: implement a small prefetch/shadow-KV buffer in runtime and measure p95 changes (by 2028-03-19).
- Rong: add packing-time padding heuristic for AWQ flows and run kernel-level microbench (by 2028-03-21).
- Samir: instrument cluster nightly job to stress-run the int8/awq workloads for 48h and collect tracer dumps (start 2028-03-18).

Why this matters for product / routing policies:
- Our routing decisions (latency-first vs cost-first) need to incorporate not just median token cost but hop-count and cache-affinity signals. A model + quant combo that looks cheap per-token can be harmful for interactive tail SLAs.
- For Dedicated and Private deployments where customers push tiny-batch interactive traffic, we should default to FP8 or adjusted AWQ packing until runtime-level mitigations land.

Appendix: quick reproduction checklist
1) Checkout runtime branch: github.com/redwood-inference/runtimes/tree/hop-instrumentation
2) Deploy to single H100 node with v2.7.1 kernel builds: make profile-build KERNELS=all
3) Use the synthetic driver: tools/loadgen/interactive_driver.py --model llm/llama2-13b --quant gptq-int8 --clients 32 --qps 300 --seq-dist 16,32,64 --trace out/trace.json
4) Upload trace to profiling tool: scripts/trace-analyze.py out/trace.json --report out/report.html

Raw notes:
- Observed one run with AWQ where an initial warmup batch produced very low p95 (~82ms) but after ~18 minutes p95 drifted up to ~160ms — correlates with a background defragmentation job on the node (we need dedicated isolation for clean baselining).
- Small heads (64) tend to trigger more fallback scalar kernels under our current int8 lane assignment.

End of draft.

(I'm leaving sections intentionally rough — this is a working doc for the team. Will convert to a polished playbook if the mitigations validate.)
